title: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
summary: Map many spellings of one company, school or title to a single ID: clean strings, block candidate pairs, score them with Fellegi-Sunter weights, cluster, and link titles to O*NET.
outcomes: Build a cleaning step with NFKC, case folding and suffix stripping, and explain what each one removes.
Compute reduction ratio and pairs completeness for a set of blocking rules.
Compute Fellegi-Sunter match weights and probabilities from m and u values and a prior.
Explain how threshold choice and connected components cause missed or false merges.
Map job titles to O*NET-SOC codes with aliases, a seniority field and embeddings, and know where each fails.

lessons.title: Why raw strings break filters and joins

blocks.md: A recruiter types the filter **company = Quantix**. Three profiles in the index really did work at Quantix, but their members typed the company as `Quantix, Inc.`, `QAUNTIX` and `Ｑｕａｎｔｉｘ Inc` (in full-width letters). An exact string filter matches none of them. The ranking can be perfect and the result is still wrong, because the right candidates never reach it.

**Entity normalization** fixes this by mapping every surface form of a real-world thing (a company, a school, a job title) to one **canonical ID**, and filtering, joining and counting on that ID. The same problem appears under many names: statisticians say **record linkage**, database people say **entity resolution** or **deduplication**, and Christen's survey lists more (merge/purge, data matching, reference reconciliation).

Two flavors share the same machinery:

1. **Linking to a reference list.** A catalog of canonical entities already exists (a company registry, a list of schools, the O*NET occupation codes) and each raw string must be mapped to one entry.
2. **Deduplication.** No catalog exists. You must decide which records refer to the same entity and invent an ID per group.

This course walks one toy dataset of 8 company records through the full pipeline: clean, block, compare, score, cluster. The last lesson applies the same ideas to job titles.

scenes.caption: Raw records arrive with case, punctuation, Unicode and suffix variation. Every later step is cheaper and more accurate if these are standardized first.
Comparing every record with every other is quadratic. Blocking keeps only pairs that share a cheap key, such as the first letters of the cleaned name.
Each candidate pair is compared field by field (name, city, domain). The result is a comparison vector: which fields agree exactly, roughly, or not at all.
A scoring model turns the comparison vector into a match weight. High scores become links, low scores are dropped, and the uncertain middle can go to a human reviewer.
Links are pairwise. Clustering turns them into groups, and each group gets one canonical ID that filters and joins use from then on.

blocks.md:
Our toy data, used in every lesson (fictional companies):

- r1 `Brightline Labs LLC`, Austin, brightline.io
- r2 `brightline labs`, Austin, TX, brightline.io
- r3 `Brightline Labs, Inc.`, Austin, no domain
- r4 `Brightline Media Inc.`, Austin, no domain
- r5 `Quantix, Inc.`, Denver, quantix.com
- r6 `QAUNTIX`, Denver, quantix.com
- r7 `Ｑｕａｎｔｉｘ Inc`, Denver, no domain
- r8 `Quanta Health`, Boulder, quantahealth.com

The truth: r1, r2, r3 are one company; r5, r6, r7 are another; r4 and r8 are distinct companies that merely look similar.

blocks.prompt: Before any normalization, how many of the 3 true Quantix records does a filter find if it compares the raw name to `quantix` case-insensitively?
blocks.reveal: **Zero.** Lowercasing `Quantix, Inc.` gives `quantix, inc.`, which still carries the suffix and comma. `QAUNTIX` has a typo. The full-width `Ｑｕａｎｔｉｘ` lowercases to full-width letters, which are different code points from ASCII. Case-insensitivity alone fixes almost nothing here.

blocks.title: Quantix records found by the filter (3 exist)

scenes.caption: Exact and case-insensitive equality both find 0 of 3. Recall on this hard filter is zero.
The cleaning pipeline of lesson 2 (Unicode NFKC, case folding, punctuation and legal-suffix removal) turns r5 and r7 into exactly `quantix`: 2 of 3.
The typo in r6 survives cleaning. Fuzzy comparison plus a second signal (the shared domain quantix.com) links it in lessons 3 to 5: 3 of 3.

blocks.md: Normalize to an ID, filter on the ID, and keep the raw string for display and debugging. Run the **same** normalizer on queries and on profiles, or the two sides drift apart and matches silently disappear.

blocks.question: A team stores only the canonical company ID and discards the raw string to save space. What goes wrong first?
options: Nothing: the canonical ID carries all the information that was in the raw string
Filters become slower because IDs are longer than names
When the matcher makes a mistake or the taxonomy changes, there is no way to audit or re-run normalization on the original input
Fuzzy matching stops working because IDs cannot be compared with edit distance
blocks.explain: Normalization is a lossy, model-driven step that will be wrong sometimes and will be improved over time. Keeping the raw string lets you show members what they typed, debug bad merges and re-normalize everything when the alias table or model changes.

blocks.question: Which situation is deduplication rather than linking to a reference list?
options: Mapping job titles to O*NET-SOC occupation codes
Grouping company names scraped from resumes when no company registry is available
Mapping school names to a fixed list of accredited universities
blocks.explain: With a reference list, each string is matched to an existing entry. Without one, you must discover the groups themselves and mint IDs for them, which is deduplication. Both use cleaning, blocking and pairwise scoring.

lessons.title: Cleaning: Unicode, case, punctuation and legal suffixes

blocks.md: Cleaning (Christen calls it *cleaning and standardisation*) converts raw input into one consistent form before anything is compared. It is deterministic, cheap and runs on every record and every query. It does not decide whether two records match; it removes differences that are never meaningful so that the later, expensive steps only see real differences.

**Unicode normalization first.** The same visible text can be stored as different code points. Unicode Standard Annex #15 defines four normalization forms. NFD and NFC handle *canonical* equivalence (for example `é` as one code point versus `e` plus a combining accent). NFKD and NFKC also apply *compatibility* mappings, which remove formatting distinctions: the `ﬁ` ligature becomes `f` and `i`, full-width letters become ASCII letters, and the Roman numeral `Ⅳ` becomes `IV`. For matching keys, NFKC is the usual choice.

**Case folding second.** Python's `str.casefold()` is like `lower()` but more aggressive, because it is meant for caseless matching: the docs' example is German `ß`, which `lower()` leaves alone and `casefold()` turns into `ss`. So `Müller Straße GmbH` and `MÜLLER STRASSE GMBH` only compare equal after casefolding.

blocks.title: Tracing clean_name on two toy records
blocks.code:
import re, unicodedata

LEGAL = {"inc", "llc", "ltd", "corp", "corporation", "co", "gmbh"}

def clean_name(raw):
    s = unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", raw)
    s = s.casefold()
    s = re.sub(r"[^\w\s]", " ", s)
    s = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", s).strip()
    tokens = [t for t in s.split() if t not in LEGAL]
    return " ".join(tokens)

clean_name("Ｑｕａｎｔｉｘ Inc")
clean_name("Brightline Labs, Inc.")

scenes.caption: Record r7 arrives in full-width letters. NFKC maps each full-width letter to its ASCII compatibility equivalent. The string is still 11 characters, but now plain ASCII.
Case folding removes case distinctions. For ASCII it is the same as lowercasing.
Punctuation becomes spaces and runs of whitespace collapse. Nothing to do for r7.
Legal-form tokens are dropped. r7 is now exactly `quantix`, identical to cleaned r5.
Record r3: NFKC changes nothing (it is already ASCII), casefold lowercases it.
The comma and the period become spaces, then whitespace collapses: `brightline labs inc`.
Dropping `inc` gives `brightline labs`, identical to cleaned r1 (`Brightline Labs LLC`) and r2.

blocks.md: After cleaning, our 8 names become: r1, r2, r3 `brightline labs`; r4 `brightline media`; r5, r7 `quantix`; r6 `qauntix`; r8 `quanta health`. Cities get the same treatment plus a small alias table (`Austin, TX` becomes `austin`; a table entry maps `sf` to `san francisco`).

blocks.prompt: Cleaning made r5 and r7 identical. What does it do for r6, `QAUNTIX`?
blocks.reveal: It becomes `qauntix`, which still differs from `quantix` by a transposition. Cleaning only removes differences that are **never** meaningful; it cannot know that `qauntix` is a typo rather than another company. That judgment needs fuzzy comparison and other fields, which is what the scoring lessons add. (From the prerequisite course: Jaro-Winkler similarity of `quantix` and `qauntix` is 0.957.)

blocks.md: **Alias tables** carry the knowledge that rules cannot derive: abbreviations (`sr` to `senior`, `swe` to `software engineer`), known nicknames and former names, and city aliases. They are simple dictionaries applied token by token or to the whole string, and they are often the highest-precision part of the system because a human wrote each entry.

Stripping is lossy. NFKC turns the superscript in `i⁹` into a plain `9`, and a stopword list that drops `group`, `bank` or `the` can merge different companies. Strip only tokens that never distinguish entities in your data, apply cleaning to the matching key, and keep the original string.
Version the normalizer. If a new suffix rule changes the key for 2% of records, every index built with the old key must be rebuilt, or queries and profiles stop matching.

blocks.question: Which single step makes `Ｑｕａｎｔｉｘ` (full-width) equal to `Quantix`?
options: Case folding with casefold()
Unicode NFC normalization
Unicode NFKC normalization
Removing punctuation
blocks.explain: Full-width letters are compatibility characters. Only the K forms (NFKD, NFKC) apply compatibility mappings; NFC handles canonical equivalence only and leaves them unchanged. Case folding does not map full-width letters to ASCII.

blocks.question: Profiles are cleaned with NFKC, casefold and suffix stripping before indexing. The query parser lowercases the recruiter's text but does nothing else. A recruiter searches `Brightline Labs, Inc.`. What happens?
options: It matches, because lowercasing is enough
It misses: the query key is `brightline labs, inc.` while the indexed key is `brightline labs`
It matches only r3, which was typed the same way
blocks.explain: The index stores cleaned keys, so a raw query string with a comma and suffix never equals them. The fix is to run the exact same normalizer on the query side.

lessons.title: Blocking: compare only pairs that could match

blocks.md: Deduplicating $n$ records means up to $n(n-1)/2$ pairs. The dedupe docs work the numbers: 1,000 records give 499,500 pairs, and 100,000 records give 4,999,950,000. Splink's docs note that 1 million records produce about 500 billion comparisons (our script: 499,999,500,000). Detailed field comparison is the bottleneck, so comparing every pair is out of the question beyond small data.

**Blocking** (Christen's survey calls the general step *indexing*) puts records into blocks by a cheap **blocking key** and compares only pairs inside a block. Christen points out the core asymmetry: comparisons grow quadratically with data size while true matches grow only linearly, so the vast majority of all pairs are non-matches that should never be compared.

blocks.caption: Christen's estimate for deduplication with b uniformly sized blocks. With n = 1,000,000 and b = 10,000 blocks: 49,500,000 pairs instead of about 500 billion. Real key values are skewed (many 'Smith'), so the largest blocks dominate.

blocks.title: Candidate pairs with and without blocking

scenes.caption: Without blocking, pairs grow with n squared: 1 million records give about 5 x 10^11 pairs.
With 1,000 equal blocks, 1 million records need about 5 x 10^8 pairs, a 1,000x cut (simplified: assumes uniform block sizes).
More, smaller blocks cut work further, but each extra split raises the chance that two true duplicates land in different blocks and are never compared.

blocks.md:
On our 8 records ($28$ possible pairs) we use two blocking rules on the *cleaned* fields, and keep a pair if **either** rule fires, as Splink does with a list of rules:

- **B1:** same first 3 characters of the cleaned name.
- **B2:** same website domain (missing domains never match).

blocks.title: Two blocking rules on the toy records

scenes.caption: 8 cleaned records, 28 possible pairs. Before cleaning, the prefixes would be `Bri`, `bri`, `Qua`, `QAU` and full-width `Ｑｕａ`, splitting true duplicates: clean before you block.
B1 (name prefix) makes blocks `bri` = {r1, r2, r3, r4}, `qua` = {r5, r7, r8} and `qau` = {r6}: 6 + 3 = 9 pairs. The typo puts r6 in a block by itself.
B2 (same domain) gives pairs r1-r2 and r5-r6. The second one is new: the domain rescues the typo record r6.
The union has 10 candidate pairs instead of 28: reduction ratio 1 - 10/28 = 0.643. Five of the 10 are true matches (pairs quality 0.5).
One true pair, r6-r7, shares no key: r6 has the typo and r7 has no domain. Pairs completeness is 5/6 = 0.833. Lesson 5 shows clustering can still recover it through r5.

blocks.md:
Christen defines three measures for the blocking step, with $s_M$ and $s_N$ the true matches and non-matches among candidate pairs, and $n_M$, $n_N$ the totals:

- **Reduction ratio** $RR = 1 - (s_M + s_N)/(n_M + n_N)$: how much work was cut. Toy: 0.643.
- **Pairs completeness** $PC = s_M / n_M$: recall of true pairs. Toy: 5/6 = 0.833.
- **Pairs quality** $PQ = s_M/(s_M + s_N)$: precision of candidates. Toy: 5/10 = 0.5.

A pair that blocking drops is classified as a non-match without ever being looked at. No scoring model can recover it. Use several strict rules joined by OR (Splink's advice: a longer list of strict rules beats a short list of loose ones), so a typo in one field is caught by a rule on another.

Libraries automate this. The dedupe library offers predicates such as *first 3 characters*, *token field* and *common 4-gram*, and learns which combination to use with a greedy set-cover algorithm that covers the labeled duplicates while keeping the comparison count low. Christen's survey compares six indexing families (traditional blocking, sorted neighbourhood, q-gram, canopy clustering, string-map and suffix-array indexing).

blocks.question: You block company records on the first 3 letters of the raw (uncleaned) name. Which true duplicate pair is most likely to be lost?
options: `Quantix, Inc.` and `Ｑｕａｎｔｉｘ Inc`
`Quantix, Inc.` and `Quantix Inc`
`Brightline Labs LLC` and `Brightline Labs, Inc.`
blocks.explain: Full-width letters are different code points, so the raw prefixes differ even though the text looks identical. The other two pairs share the raw prefix `Qua` or `Bri`. Blocking keys must be computed from cleaned values.

blocks.question: Adding a third rule, *same city*, to our toy blocking would do what?
options: Raise pairs completeness to 1.0 and keep the candidate count at 10
Recover r6-r7 (both Denver) but add many more pairs, lowering the reduction ratio
Have no effect, because city is not a name field
blocks.explain: City is low-cardinality: everyone in Austin would be paired with everyone else in Austin. It recovers r6-r7 but at a large cost in comparisons on real data. A stricter combined key (city plus name prefix of 2 letters, say) is the usual compromise.

lessons.title: Scoring pairs with Fellegi-Sunter match weights

blocks.md: For each candidate pair we compare fields and record a **comparison vector** $\gamma$: for example name *exact*, city *exact*, domain *missing*. Splink calls each field's test a *comparison* with ordered **comparison levels**, checked like an if/elif chain (its docs example: exact match, Jaro-Winkler above 0.95, above 0.8, everything else). We use three: name (exact, Jaro-Winkler at least 0.88, else), city (exact, else) and domain (exact, else, or no evidence if missing).

Fellegi and Sunter (1969) framed linkage as hypothesis testing. Each level has two probabilities:

- $m$ = P(this level | the records truly match). It measures data quality: true duplicates agree on city most of the time, but typos and moves happen.
- $u$ = P(this level | the records do not match). It measures coincidence: two unrelated companies share a city far more often than a website domain.

blocks.caption: Splink's form. Each field adds its weight w; the prior lambda is the probability that two random records match. Adding weights assumes fields are independent given match status.

blocks.md:
Assumed parameters for the toy (illustrative values of the kind Splink estimates: $u$ from random record pairs, which are almost all non-matches, and $m$ by expectation maximisation on blocked pairs):

- name: exact $m$=0.70, $u$=0.002 (w = 8.45); fuzzy 0.25, 0.01 (w = 4.64); else 0.05, 0.988 (w = -4.30)
- city: exact 0.90, 0.05 (w = 4.17); else 0.10, 0.95 (w = -3.25)
- domain: exact 0.85, 0.001 (w = 9.73); else 0.15, 0.999 (w = -2.74); missing: w = 0
- prior $\lambda$ = 0.001, so the prior weight is $\log_2(0.001/0.999) = -9.96$

blocks.prompt: r1 and r3 have the same cleaned name and city, but r3 has no domain. Using the weights above, is the match probability above or below 0.95?
blocks.reveal: **Below: 0.863.** The weight is -9.96 + 8.45 + 4.17 + 0 = 2.66, and $2^{2.66}/(1+2^{2.66}) = 0.863$. Agreement on name and city is strong evidence, but it must overcome a prior of 1 in 1,000. Without the domain there is not enough evidence to be 95% sure.

blocks.title: Match weight, one field at a time

scenes.caption: r1-r2: every field agrees exactly. Total 12.39, probability 0.9998. (Bars show size; the number shows the sign.)
r1-r3: same name and city, domain missing, so it adds 0. Total 2.66, probability 0.863: likely but not certain.
r5-r6: the typo drops name to the fuzzy level (4.64 instead of 8.45), but the shared domain adds 9.73. Total 8.58, probability 0.997.
r1-r4 (labs vs media, Jaro-Winkler 0.91): fuzzy name plus same city, no domain. Total -1.15, probability 0.311. Different companies, but the evidence is thin.
r5-r8: name, city and domain all disagree. Total -20.25, probability about 0.0000008.
Per-field weights for each candidate pair (total includes the -9.96 prior). Red-blue scale: positive is evidence for a match.
Seven pairs have a missing domain, so that column contributes 0 and they lean entirely on name and city.
Totals: r1-r2 (12.39) and r5-r6 (8.58) are clear links; r5-r8 and r7-r8 are clear non-links; the 2.66 and -1.15 rows are the uncertain middle.

blocks.md: Fellegi and Sunter's decision rule has **three** outcomes, not two: *link*, *non-link* and *possible link*. Sort pairs by weight, choose an upper threshold for an acceptable false-link rate and a lower threshold for an acceptable missed-link rate, and send everything in between to clerical review. Their theorem shows this rule minimizes the number of possible links (human work) for the chosen error levels.

blocks.title: From summed evidence to match probability

scenes.caption: With prior -9.96, the evidence must sum to 14.2 to reach P = 0.95. Only r1-r2 and r5-r6 clear the accept line.
r1-r3, r2-r3, r5-r7 (0.863) and r1-r4, r2-r4, r3-r4 (0.311) sit between the lines: 6 of 10 pairs go to review, mostly because the domain is missing.

Raise the prior to -6.63 (lambda = 0.01) and the curve shifts left. The plotted points do not move with the slider: they were computed at lambda = 0.001. The prior encodes how rare matches are in the data.

blocks.md: The independence assumption double-counts correlated fields. Company name and website domain usually agree or disagree together, so adding both full weights overstates the evidence. Merge strongly correlated fields into one comparison, or check calibration on labeled pairs.
Each field adds $\log_2(m/u)$. Agreement on a rare value (a domain) is worth far more than agreement on a common one (a city), and a missing field adds nothing instead of counting as a disagreement.

blocks.question: City has m = 0.90 and u = 0.05 for exact agreement. A new data source has many members who typed their home city instead of the company's HQ city, so true duplicates agree on city only 45% of the time. What happens to the exact-city weight?
options: It stays 4.17 because u did not change
It drops to log2(0.45/0.05) = 3.17
It becomes negative
It doubles, because more disagreement means more information
blocks.explain: m measures how often true matches agree. Halving m from 0.90 to 0.45 subtracts exactly 1 from log2(m/u). Disagreement also becomes less damning: the else weight rises from log2(0.10/0.95) = -3.25 to log2(0.55/0.95) = -0.79.

blocks.question: Why is a missing domain scored as weight 0 rather than with the disagree weight -2.74?
options: Missing data carries no evidence either way; scoring it as disagreement would push true duplicates like r1-r3 toward non-match
Because log2 of zero is undefined
Because Fellegi-Sunter only allows agreement levels
blocks.explain: A missing value is neither agreement nor disagreement. Treating it as disagreement subtracts 2.74 and would drop r1-r3 from 0.863 to about 0.49, punishing incomplete records rather than conflicting ones.

lessons.title: From pairwise links to entities: clustering

blocks.md: Scores are about **pairs**, but we need **groups**: one canonical ID per real company. The simplest method, used by Splink's `cluster_pairwise_predictions_at_threshold`, is **connected components**: keep every pair with probability at or above a threshold as an edge, and each connected group of records becomes one cluster.

Connected components are transitive by construction: if r5 links to r6 and r5 links to r7, then r6 and r7 end up together even if they were never compared. That rescues pairs that blocking missed, and it is also the main danger, because a single wrong edge merges two whole clusters.

scenes.caption: Edge labels show each candidate pair's match probability from lesson 4. r6-r7 (dashed) was never compared, so it has no score.
Threshold 0.95 keeps only r1-r2 and r5-r6. Six clusters: r3 and r7 are left alone. Pairwise precision 1.0, recall 2/6 = 0.33.
Threshold 0.8 adds the three 0.863 edges. Four clusters, exactly the truth. r6 and r7 join through r5 although they were never compared: precision 1.0, recall 1.0.
Threshold 0.3 also accepts the 0.311 edges to r4. Brightline Media is merged into Brightline Labs: the cluster implies 6 pairs, 3 of them wrong. Precision 6/9 = 0.67.

blocks.title: Pairwise precision and recall of the clusters

scenes.caption: Threshold 0.95: every implied pair is right, but only 2 of 6 true pairs are found.
Threshold 0.8: all 6 true pairs found and no false ones on this toy data.
Threshold 0.3: recall stays 1.0 but 3 of the 9 implied pairs are false.

blocks.prompt: r6-r7 has the same comparison vector as r1-r4: fuzzy name, same city, no domain, probability 0.311. One is a true match, the other is not. What does this tell you?
blocks.reveal: The model cannot tell them apart: **identical evidence gives identical scores**. On these three fields, a typo of the same company and a different company with a similar name look the same. Only more evidence (another field, a labeled example, a reviewer) or transitivity through a third record can separate them. Here r6-r7 is rescued by r5; r1-r4 should stay out.

blocks.md: The dedupe docs give the classic warning: if A-B and B-C each have a 60% match probability, A-C is only about 36% likely, so pairwise probabilities are not transitive. dedupe therefore uses hierarchical clustering with centroid linkage instead of plain connected components, and lets you pick the threshold. Whatever the method, evaluate on labeled clusters and report pairwise precision and recall.

Once clusters exist, each gets a stable **canonical ID** and a display name. A common choice is the most frequent cleaned name or the most complete record in the cluster. New records are then linked to existing clusters (the reference-list case) instead of re-clustering everything, so IDs used in filters and analytics do not churn.

Watch cluster sizes. One low-threshold edge between two big clusters creates a giant cluster that silently merges thousands of records. Alert on clusters that grow suddenly, and require stronger evidence for edges that would join two large clusters.

Blocking decides which pairs are compared, scoring decides which pairs are linked, and clustering decides which records share an ID. Tune the threshold on labeled data, because it trades false merges against missed merges.

blocks.question: Using our scores, which threshold gives perfect clusters on the toy data?
options: Any threshold between 0.311 and 0.863, such as 0.8
No threshold, because r6-r7 was never compared
blocks.explain: Any threshold above 0.311 and at most 0.863 accepts the five true edges and rejects the r4 edges. r6-r7 is not needed as a direct edge: connected components join r6 and r7 through r5.

blocks.question: Your entity graph has a cluster of 40,000 company records that should be about 30 companies. What is the most likely cause?
options: Blocking was too strict
A few false links between large clusters, chained by transitive connected components
The prior lambda was set too low
blocks.explain: Strict blocking and a low prior both cause missed links, which make clusters too small. Giant clusters come from false edges: connected components chains them, so one bad edge between two big clusters merges both.

lessons.title: Job titles: taxonomies, seniority and embeddings

blocks.md:
Companies and schools are mostly a dedup problem. **Job titles** are usually linked to a reference **taxonomy**, because titles that differ in words can mean the same job. Two public taxonomies are common:

- **O*NET-SOC 2019** (US Department of Labor): 1,016 occupations, coded by the SOC hierarchy plus a two-digit O*NET extension. Its [Alternate Titles](https://www.onetcenter.org/dictionary/30.1/mssql/alternate_titles.html) file (56,505 rows in release 30.1) maps titles people use to codes.
- **ESCO** (European Commission): takes its top four levels from ISCO-08, maps each occupation to exactly one ISCO-08 code, and stores preferred and non-preferred terms across its 28 languages.

blocks.title: From a typed title to an O*NET-SOC code

scenes.caption: The member typed `Sr. SWE II`. No taxonomy lists that string.
An abbreviation table expands `sr` and `swe`; seniority tokens (`senior`, `II`) go to a separate field. What is left is the core title `software engineer`.
O*NET lists Software Engineer among the reported titles for 15-1252.00 Software Developers, so an alias lookup assigns that code.

The code sits in a hierarchy (shown: major group, broad group 15-1250 Software and Web Developers, Programmers, and Testers, detailed occupation; minor group 15-1200 omitted), so filters can widen from one occupation to a whole family.

blocks.md: Keeping seniority separate matters for search: a filter for *software developers* should match `Staff Software Engineer` and `Junior Developer`, while a separate seniority filter handles level. LinkedIn's engineering blog describes the same shape at scale: a title taxonomy (24K titles in 19 languages when the post was written) where similar titles roll up into a *supertitle* and supertitles into a *function* such as Engineering. Synonym phrases were found by clustering word2vec vectors and then validated by human taxonomists.

When no alias matches, **sentence embeddings** help. Sentence-BERT trains a siamese network so that cosine similarity of two sentence vectors reflects meaning; its paper reports finding the most similar pair among 10,000 sentences in about 5 seconds instead of about 65 hours with a BERT cross-encoder. You embed every taxonomy label and alternate title once, then embed each incoming title and take the nearest label (or use the top few as candidates, a form of blocking).

blocks.title: Cosine similarity of titles to O*NET occupations

scenes.caption: Raw titles vs occupation names (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, computed). Abbreviations score near noise: `Sr. SWE II` peaks at 0.25. `Software Eng. in Test` picks Software Developers (0.53) over QA (0.50): wrong.
After abbreviation expansion and seniority stripping, `software engineer` scores 0.82 and `registered nurse` 0.96. The test-engineer rows still lean the wrong way (0.68 and 0.65 vs 0.60).
Compare against each occupation's name plus O*NET reported titles and take the best. Both test rows now pick QA (0.92 and 0.96, via Software Test Engineer). Every row is right.

blocks.md: Read the last scene carefully. `Sales Engineer` scores 0.69 against `Software Engineer`, and `software engineer` scores 0.83 against `Software Test Engineer`: the gap between right and wrong is often 0.1 to 0.2. Embeddings rank candidates well but are poor at saying *no*. Production systems therefore combine them: aliases and rules first, embeddings to propose the top few codes, then a threshold on the margin or a classifier (or an LLM restricted to a fixed list of IDs) to decide.

General-purpose embedding models do not know your abbreviations (`SWE`, `SDET`, `RN`) and blur words that share context (`sales engineer` vs `software engineer`). Expand abbreviations before embedding, match against many alternate titles rather than one label, and keep an *unknown* outcome instead of forcing the nearest code.

The same pattern works for schools and companies: an alias table for known variants (`MIT`), Fellegi-Sunter or a trained classifier for record pairs, embeddings to generate candidates, and a review queue for the uncertain middle.

blocks.question: A raw title `Sr SDET` must map to an O*NET code. Which pipeline gets it right in the computed example?
options: Embed the raw string and take the nearest occupation name
Lowercase, then exact lookup in the occupation names
Expand abbreviations, strip seniority, then match against occupation names plus alternate titles
Strip seniority only, then embed and take the nearest occupation name
blocks.explain: Raw abbreviations score near noise (`SDET` peaks at 0.25), and an exact lookup never finds `sr sdet`. Even after expansion, the occupation name alone picks Software Developers (0.68 vs 0.60). Matching against reported titles such as Software Test Engineer gives QA at 0.92.

blocks.question: Why store seniority in a separate field instead of making `Senior Software Engineer` its own taxonomy entry?
options: Taxonomies cannot store adjectives
So that an occupation filter matches every level, and level can be filtered independently, without multiplying entries per occupation
Because embeddings cannot encode seniority
blocks.explain: Combining occupation and level multiplies entries and splits recall: a filter for software developers would have to enumerate every level. Two fields keep both filters simple and avoid one taxonomy entry per occupation and level.
